hints: Look closely at the three positions on glycerol, top, middle and bottom. What happens if you flip the whole triglyceride upside down?
The top and bottom positions are equivalent when the molecule rotates, so only the fatty acid in the middle (position 2) makes a truly new type. How many choices are there for that middle spot?
walkthrough:
**Spot the three slots**

Think of glycerol as having three hooks for fatty acids, top, middle and bottom. We must place one L, one O and one P, using each exactly once.

At first you might think: $3 \times 2 \times 1 = 6$ ways.

**Remember the molecule can flip**

A triglyceride is not fixed up or down in space. If you turn it 180 degrees, what was top becomes bottom and what was bottom becomes top.

That means L-O-P with L on top and P at the bottom is the same molecule as P-O-L with P on top and L at the bottom.

**Count only the middle fatty acid**

The middle position never changes when you flip, so it is the only one that defines a new type. There are just 3 choices for the middle: L in the middle, O in the middle, or P in the middle.

So total different arrangements = $3$.

options.A: Correct. There are only 3 unique types, decided by which acid (L, O or P) occupies the middle position, because top and bottom swap on flipping.
options.B: Not 4. There is no fourth unique middle position, there are only three fatty acids to put there.
options.C: Not 5. This adds extra types that do not exist once flipped duplicates are removed.
options.D: Not 9. That would be $3 \times 3 \times 3$, which allows repeats of the same acid, but here we must use one L, one O and one P.
